subtopic_detail: Progressive disinhibition and apathy with preserved memory at sixty
stem:
A 60 year old accountant is brought to your clinic by his wife, who has had to take over the household finances. Over two years he has made a series of uncharacteristic remarks to strangers, began eating large quantities of sweet food, and now sits for hours without initiating anything.

His wife says he still remembers appointments, finds his way around without difficulty and can recount last week's events accurately. He shows no concern about any of the changes. Formal cognitive testing shows preserved orientation and delayed recall, with marked impairment of planning, set shifting and response inhibition. There is no tremor, no rigidity, no gait disturbance and no visual hallucination. Magnetic resonance imaging shows asymmetric frontal and anterior temporal atrophy with no vascular lesion.

data_table.Examination: Disinhibited in interview, no insight, no parkinsonian signs, normal gait, primitive reflexes present, no focal deficit
data_table.Cognitive testing: Orientation and delayed recall preserved, marked impairment of planning, set shifting and response inhibition
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function, liver function, thyroid function, B12 and syphilis serology all within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Magnetic resonance imaging shows asymmetric frontal and anterior temporal atrophy without vascular lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start donepezil and refer him to a memory service for follow up
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are not effective in this disorder and frequently worsen behavioural symptoms and agitation, because the cholinergic deficit that underlies their benefit in Alzheimer disease is not the pathology here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start risperidone to control the disinhibited behaviour long term
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are used sparingly and briefly for severe behavioural disturbance, and long term use in any dementia carries increased stroke and mortality risk, so it is not the primary management strategy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer to a cognitive service and avoid a cholinesterase inhibitor
options.rationale: Early onset dementia with prominent behavioural change, loss of insight, dietary change and executive impairment while memory and navigation are preserved, alongside asymmetric frontotemporal atrophy, indicates behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia. Management is specialist assessment with behavioural and caregiver support, and cholinesterase inhibitors are specifically avoided because they can worsen behaviour. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer to psychiatry for treatment of a presumed depressive disorder
options.rationale: Apathy is easily mistaken for depression and this diagnosis is frequently made first, but he has no subjective low mood, no guilt and no sleep or appetite loss in the usual pattern, and the imaging shows structural disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure the couple and repeat his cognitive testing in twelve months
options.rationale: A two year progressive course with objective executive impairment and unequivocal atrophy on imaging is established disease, and delay costs the family the practical, financial and legal planning that early diagnosis permits. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia typically begins between 45 and 65 years and is distinguished from Alzheimer disease by the early and dominant change in personality and social conduct while episodic memory and spatial navigation remain relatively preserved. Characteristic features include disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive or ritualised behaviour, marked change in eating with a preference for sweet foods, and profound loss of insight. Because insight is absent, the history almost always comes from a family member. Cholinesterase inhibitors are not indicated and can worsen behavioural symptoms, so management centres on specialist diagnosis, non pharmacological behavioural strategies, caregiver support, and early attention to driving, financial capacity and advance planning.
key_points: Preserved memory and navigation with prominent behavioural change is the pattern that separates it from Alzheimer disease
Loss of insight means collateral history is essential
Cholinesterase inhibitors are ineffective and may worsen behaviour
Early diagnosis enables decisions about driving, work and financial capacity while some capacity remains
explanation.pearls: Address driving and financial capacity at the first consultation rather than at review: disinhibition and impaired judgement with absent insight make these patients dangerous on the road and vulnerable to financial exploitation well before their memory scores fall.

subtopic_detail: Erythema nodosum with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and ankle arthritis
stem:
A 32 year old woman attends your clinic with two weeks of painful red lumps on both shins, aching swollen ankles and a low grade fever. She has a mild dry cough but is not breathless and can still run for the bus.

She was born in Australia, has never smoked, has had no tuberculosis contact and has not travelled overseas. A chest radiograph arranged by her general practitioner shows symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields and no parenchymal infiltrate. Her spirometry, including gas transfer, is normal. Serum calcium and creatinine are normal, her electrocardiogram is normal, and ophthalmology review today found no uveitis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tender erythematous nodules over both shins, bilateral ankle swelling and tenderness, chest clear on auscultation, no lymphadenopathy elsewhere, no skin plaques
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), angiotensin converting enzyme raised, interferon gamma release assay negative, spirometry with gas transfer within normal limits, electrocardiogram normal
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start high dose oral prednisolone and taper it over six months
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is indicated for progressive pulmonary disease, hypercalcaemia, cardiac, neurological or sight threatening ocular involvement, none of which is present, and it exposes a woman with a self limiting illness to months of avoidable adverse effects. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Start standard four drug antituberculous therapy and notify the case
options.rationale: Tuberculosis causes hilar lymphadenopathy but characteristically asymmetric or unilateral, and her interferon gamma release assay is negative with no exposure history and no risk factors. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange mediastinal lymph node biopsy to confirm the diagnosis first
options.rationale: Tissue confirmation is required for atypical presentations, but this triad is considered sufficiently characteristic that biopsy is not needed, and the procedure carries risk without changing management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Treat with a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug and observe her
options.rationale: The combination of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, ankle arthritis and fever is an acute presentation of sarcoidosis that remits spontaneously in the large majority of patients within one to two years, so symptomatic treatment with an anti inflammatory drug and structured observation is appropriate. Systemic corticosteroid is reserved for organ threatening disease, which she does not have. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Start methotrexate as a steroid sparing agent and review in one month
options.rationale: Second line immunosuppression is for chronic disease requiring prolonged corticosteroid or for steroid failure, and starting it in an illness that usually resolves by itself is disproportionate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: The acute syndrome of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, arthritis and fever is a recognised presentation of sarcoidosis with an excellent prognosis, remitting spontaneously in the great majority of patients. It is one of the few settings in which the diagnosis is accepted on clinical and radiological grounds without tissue confirmation. The treatment decision is therefore not which immunosuppressant to use but whether to treat at all, and the answer for uncomplicated disease is symptomatic management with observation. Corticosteroids are reserved for organ threatening involvement, meaning progressive pulmonary impairment, hypercalcaemia, cardiac, neurological or sight threatening ocular disease.
key_points: Symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields distinguishes this from tuberculosis and lymphoma
Biopsy is not required when the clinical picture is characteristic
Baseline assessment includes calcium, renal function, electrocardiogram, spirometry with gas transfer and ophthalmology review
Serum angiotensin converting enzyme is neither sensitive nor specific and should not drive treatment decisions
explanation.pearls: The electrocardiogram and the eye review are the two easily forgotten parts of the baseline workup: cardiac sarcoidosis can present with nothing more than conduction delay, and asymptomatic uveitis found on slit lamp examination converts an observe only plan into one requiring treatment.

subtopic_detail: Thyrotoxicosis with absent vascularity on Doppler in a man taking amiodarone
stem:
A 67 year old man attends your clinic with three months of weight loss of 8 kg, heat intolerance and worsening palpitations. He has taken amiodarone for two years for recurrent atrial fibrillation after other agents failed, and his rhythm had been well controlled until recently.

He has no eye signs, no goitre and no thyroid bruit. He has no family history of thyroid disease and has had no recent iodinated contrast. His thyroid stimulating hormone is suppressed with a raised free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine. Thyroid receptor antibodies are negative. Colour flow Doppler ultrasound of the thyroid shows a normal sized gland with markedly reduced vascularity throughout.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 148/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, warm peripheries, no goitre, no thyroid bruit, no proptosis or lid lag, irregularly irregular pulse
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 42 pmol/L (10-25), free triiodothyronine raised, thyroid receptor antibodies negative, C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Imaging: Colour flow Doppler shows a normal sized gland with markedly reduced vascularity throughout

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start carbimazole and arrange endocrinology and cardiology review
options.rationale: Thionamides block new hormone synthesis and are effective in the iodine induced form, which shows increased vascularity in a nodular or enlarged gland. They have little effect when preformed hormone is being released from a destroyed gland. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange radioactive iodine treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed
options.rationale: Iodine uptake is profoundly suppressed by the large iodine load from amiodarone, so radioiodine cannot be delivered to the gland and the treatment is ineffective in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Stop the amiodarone alone and recheck his thyroid function in a month
options.rationale: Cessation may be appropriate but amiodarone has a half life of many weeks so withdrawal alone does not control thyrotoxicosis in the short term, and stopping it can destabilise the arrhythmia it was prescribed for. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start potassium iodide and arrange urgent total thyroidectomy
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for severe disease failing medical therapy or requiring rapid control in a patient who cannot stop amiodarone, and adding further iodine to an already iodine loaded patient is counterproductive. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start prednisolone and arrange endocrinology and cardiology review
options.rationale: Absent vascularity on colour flow Doppler with negative receptor antibodies and no goitre indicates a destructive thyroiditis releasing preformed hormone rather than increased synthesis, and this form responds to corticosteroid rather than to thionamides. Joint endocrine and cardiology input is needed because the decision about continuing amiodarone depends on the arrhythmia risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Amiodarone contains a large iodine load and causes thyroid dysfunction in a significant minority of patients, and distinguishing the two forms of thyrotoxicosis it produces determines the treatment. The iodine induced form arises in a gland with underlying nodularity or latent autoimmune disease, involves excess synthesis, shows preserved or increased vascularity on colour flow Doppler, and responds to thionamides. The destructive form occurs in a structurally normal gland, releases preformed hormone from damaged follicles, shows absent vascularity, and responds to corticosteroid. Mixed forms occur and are treated with both. Whether to continue amiodarone is a joint decision with cardiology, since its long half life means cessation gives no rapid benefit.
key_points: Colour flow Doppler vascularity is the practical discriminator between the two forms
Radioiodine is ineffective because the iodine load suppresses uptake
Amiodarone has a half life of weeks, so stopping it does not achieve short term control
Amiodarone more commonly causes hypothyroidism, which is treated with thyroxine while the drug continues
explanation.pearls: Do not assume stopping amiodarone is the answer: in a patient whose arrhythmia was refractory to everything else, withdrawal may precipitate the very rhythm disturbance that a thyrotoxic heart tolerates worst, and the decision belongs jointly with cardiology.
